title: Mega-Cap Tech Stocks Fall 7% Following Deutsche Bank Downgrade
text: Markets Mega-Cap Tech Stocks Fall 7% Following Deutsche Bank Downgrade A well-timed tactical call by a major Wall Street research team preceded a broad selloff in US technology equities, raising questions about whether the sector has found a floor. Gab-E Intelligence Platform · October 26, 2026 Mega-cap growth and technology stocks listed on US exchanges fell approximately 7% in the weeks following a tactical downgrade issued by Deutsche Bank on October 9, 2026, according to analysis published by MacroBusiness . The decline represents one of the more significant sector-level pullbacks of the current market cycle in US-listed technology equities. Deutsche Bank strategist Binky Chadha and his team issued the downgrade on October 9, moving their rating on the technology sector from overweight to neutral, according to the MacroBusiness report. The note cited an unfavorable risk-to-reward setup and warned of the potential for a sharp reversal in prices. The 7% figure refers to the cumulative price decline in mega-cap growth and technology stocks between the date of the downgrade and the date of the MacroBusiness analysis. The source does not specify which index or basket of securities was used to calculate that figure, and the precise composition of the referenced cohort is not independently confirmed in the available source material. The MacroBusiness report frames the decline as an "AI crash," a term referencing the concentrated losses in companies whose valuations had been supported in part by investor expectations for artificial intelligence-related revenue growth. The report does not define a specific threshold for what constitutes an AI crash, nor does it cite earnings data to support a fundamental deterioration in those companies' results. US technology stocks, particularly large-cap names in the S&P 500 Information Technology sector, had outperformed the broader index significantly in 2024 and 2025. The iShares S&P 500 Information Technology Sector ETF (IXN) and similar instruments track these names, though the MacroBusiness source does not specify which vehicle or index it used to measure the 7% decline. The Chadha downgrade came roughly two weeks before the current date of October 26, 2026. Whether the decline represents a temporary correction or a longer-term trend reversal is unknown. What would clarify that question is the next round of earnings reports from major US technology companies, which would reveal whether revenue and guidance figures justify current valuations at their post-decline levels. Sector-level downgrades from major research teams do not themselves cause price movements, but they can amplify selling pressure when they coincide with existing investor caution. The MacroBusiness report credits Deutsche Bank's timing as precise, though it does not quantify how much of the 7% decline occurred in the days immediately following the note versus over a longer period. US investors with exposure to broad market index funds or technology-focused exchange-traded funds are directly affected by this sector drawdown, as information technology remains the largest sector weight in the S&P 500 by market capitalization, according to S&P Dow Jones Indices data. Any sustained decline in mega-cap technology names has a proportionally larger effect on passive investors holding cap-weighted index products. The MacroBusiness report poses the question of whether the decline is over but does not answer it with data. The next set of observable signals would include forward price-to-earnings ratios for the sector, Federal Reserve commentary on financial conditions, and earnings guidance from companies such as Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Alphabet, all of which report quarterly results on schedules published in their investor relations filings. The broader US stock market context for this selloff is not fully described in the available source material. It is not confirmed whether the technology decline was accompanied by rotation into other sectors or by broad market weakness across all S&P 500 industries. That information would be available through daily market data published by exchanges including the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq.
